featured_techniques.technique: Eliminate internal airline jargon to improve external customer service
Reframe staff-facing terminology to reflect customer-centric values (e.g., guests vs. passengers)
Leadership/branding through changed executive language (e.g., 'big shots' as a contrast to guest-centric terms)
Cultural transformation as a strategic driver of competitive advantage

locations.basis: Transcript explicitly refers to WestJet as a Canadian airline and mentions Canadians
locations.name: Canada

concepts: language as a driver of brand perception
sections.description: Opening idea: the way a company is heard about online depends on the language used in meetings and internal communications, framing how outsiders perceive the business.
sections.title: Perception and the power of organizational language

sections.description: Illustrates how airline staff may use shorthand (e.g., pax in seat 10 wants a coffee) that can leak into customer interactions if not managed.
sections.title: Flight-crew shorthand as an example of internal lingo

sections.description: WestJet decided to get rid of the old lingo and shift toward a respectful, guest-centric approach. They frame customers as honored guests, and the ensuing attitude is described as permeating the organization. The result, framed as a five-year outcome, was that WestJet surpassed other Canadian airlines to become the second-largest carrier in Canada.
sections.title: WestJet’s lingo reform and its consequences

summary: The speaker uses a concrete industry example to illustrate how internal language shapes customer experience and brand perception. By showing flight-crew shorthand (such as Pax in seat 10 wants a coffee) and WestJet’s deliberate move to eliminate that lingo, the talk demonstrates a shift toward a guest-centric service culture. The new attitude—treating passengers as honored guests—permeates the organization and is linked to a dramatic competitive outcome in the Canadian market within five years. The excerpt highlights how language choices at the leadership and daily operations level can become a strategic lever for differentiation.
title: WestJet Lingo Reform: From Flight-Attendant Slang to Honored Guest Service
